nameStory: The hairy spiny dorid gets its descriptive name from the tiny spines and hair-like projections that cover its soft body, giving it a fuzzy, textured appearance. 'Dorid' refers to a major group of sea slugs that have their gills arranged in a circle around their back end, like a living flower.
description: The hairy spiny dorid is a shell-less sea slug that crawls along the ocean floor like a miniature underwater cow. These soft-bodied marine animals are nudibranchs, meaning 'naked gills' - you can actually see their feathery breathing organs on their backs. Their bodies are covered in tiny spines and hair-like bumps that give them a distinctly fuzzy texture. They typically grow to about an inch or two in length and come in mottled colors that help them blend with their surroundings.

idTips.label: Fuzzy texture
idTips.description: The entire body feels rough and bumpy to gentle touch, covered in tiny spines and hair-like projections that create a distinctly textured surface unlike smooth sea slugs

idTips.label: Circular gill cluster
idTips.description: Feathery, flower-like gills form a perfect circle around the back end of the animal, retracting when disturbed and expanding when the animal feels safe

idTips.label: Mottled coloration
idTips.description: Body shows irregular patches of browns, grays, and sometimes reddish tones that help it blend with rocky surfaces and marine growth

idTips.label: Two tentacle-like projections
idTips.description: A pair of horn-like sensory organs stick up from the front of the head, often with ridged or wrinkled surfaces that help detect chemicals in the water

idTips.label: Crawling movement
idTips.description: Moves very slowly across surfaces using its muscular foot, leaving a slight slime trail and often pausing to feed on sponges and other growth

habitat: Look for hairy spiny dorids in shallow coastal waters along rocky shores, tide pools, and areas with plenty of marine growth. They prefer spots where sponges grow abundantly since these make up their primary food source. You'll most often spot them during low tides when they're exposed in tide pools or clinging to the undersides of rocks and pier pilings.

seasonality.spring: Most active as water temperatures begin to warm, often found feeding on newly growing sponges in shallow areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're easiest to spot during low tides, moving more actively across tide pool surfaces to feed and potentially mate.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to slightly deeper waters, though still findable in protected tide pools during very low tides.
seasonality.winter: Much less active and harder to find, typically in deeper water or well-protected crevices where they wait out the coldest months.

funFact: When threatened, the hairy spiny dorid can actually shed and regrow its beautiful circular gill cluster - imagine being able to drop and regrow your lungs as an escape strategy!
confusionNotes: Could be mistaken for other dorid nudibranchs, but the distinctly hairy, spiny texture is unique - run your finger gently over it and you'll feel the difference immediately, while other sea slugs feel smooth or just bumpy.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gill' in Latin, referring to how these sea slugs wear their breathing organs on the outside of their bodies like living decorations, unlike most marine animals that hide their gills inside shells or body cavities.
compareHints: Since this is the only Acanthodoris species commonly found in New England waters, compare it with other dorid nudibranchs by feeling for its signature hairy texture. Other dorids in the region tend to have smooth skin or simple bumps, while the hairy spiny dorid feels distinctly fuzzy and rough to the touch.
